In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[group theory]], a [[group (mathematics)|group]] is said to be '''strictly simple''' if it has no proper nontrivial [[ascendant subgroup]]s. That is, <math>G</math> is a strictly simple group if the only ascendant subgroups of <math>G</math> are <math>\{ e \}</math> (the trivial subgroup), and <math>G</math> itself (the whole group).

In the finite case, a group is strictly simple if and only if it is [[simple group|simple]]. However, in the infinite case, strictly simple is a stronger property than simple.
